questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a wood panel is coated before painting
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose of a gesso ground on a wooden panel
questions.stem: A panel painter gessoes a plank of wood, mixing powdered chalk or gypsum with an animal-glue size and laying it in thin layers, before any paint touches the surface. What does that coating achieve?

options.text: It supplies a flat, bright and absorbent surface, so a design can be drawn and colour applied without the raw wood swallowing the binder
It locks the grain in place, so the plank can no longer expand or contract and is thereby protected from splitting
options.misconception: believes the gesso halts the movement of the wood, when a rigid ground only splits when the support moves

options.text: It carries the underdrawing, since the design is brushed into the wet gesso and becomes part of the ground itself
options.misconception: thinks the gesso itself bears the design, confusing a prepared ground with a drawing laid over it

options.text: It gives the finished surface its shine, so that the picture needs no varnish and no later protective coating at all
options.misconception: assumes a chalk ground produces the gloss, when sheen comes from a varnish or an oil film

questions.explanation: Bare wood is uneven, absorbent and full of knots, and it drinks the binder out of any paint applied straight onto it, which leaves the colour thin, patchy and unable to take a drawn line. Ground chalk or gypsum suspended in glue gives a surface that is level, porous enough to grip paint, and pale enough that the painter's own tones decide the value of the picture rather than the colour of the wood. The layers are laid thin and dried and sanded between coats so that the ground hardens without cracking, and the gesso is then often toned so the design reads against it. The other jobs people assign to it are not the ground's work: the grain still moves underneath, the drawing is a separate layer on top, and gloss is supplied later by varnish or by a resinous medium.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the binder of a paint layer if the raw timber is the only thing underneath it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: identify the working function of a painting ground
questions.stem: In panel and canvas painting a ground is the layer between the support and the first paint. Which of these is something a ground actually does for the painter?

options.text: It provides an even field of one tone, so light and shadow can be modelled and judged as values
It supplies the picture's final colour, because the ground is mixed with enough pigment to set the hue
options.misconception: thinks the ground is the source of colour, when it is a neutral or faintly tinted preparation

options.text: It forms the varnish film, since the ground is the last coating before the frame and takes the polish
options.misconception: confuses the ground with the varnish, which is a separate layer applied at the end

options.text: It creates the craquelure, because a thick ground cracks as the support moves and sets the pattern
options.misconception: believes the ground causes all cracking, when a moving wooden support is the usual source

questions.explanation: A ground exists so that the painter is not working on a moving, absorbent and uneven surface. Its practical value is that it gives a single starting value across the whole picture, which is what makes it possible to judge a highlight as lighter than its neighbour or a shadow as darker. It also grips the first paint film instead of letting the support absorb it, and its thickness can be built and sanded until the surface will take a fine line. It is normally not the source of the picture's colour, though grounds were often toned, and that tone is meant to read through the paint as a warmth rather than to be seen as a colour in itself. It is not the varnish, which is a separate protective film applied last, and it is not the origin of the crack network, which usually follows the wood's own movement under a ground that is far stiffer than itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the painter needs to know about the picture before the first colour goes down.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an underdrawing is for
questions.learningObjective: state the working role of an underdrawing in a finished painting
questions.stem: Infrared or X-ray examination of a fifteenth-century panel painting reveals a drawing beneath the paint layer. What was that underdrawing doing while the picture was being made?

options.text: It settled the design and its proportions in advance, so colour was applied to a composition already decided
It recorded light and shadow in outline, so the finished highlights and darks could be traced from it
options.misconception: assumes the underdrawing was a shading study, when it carries the composition

options.text: It supplied warm tones that glow through thin paint and so acts as a coloured shadow
options.misconception: calls an underdrawing an imprimatura, confusing a drawn design with a tinted ground

options.text: It authenticated the picture, because a competent hand cannot imitate another's transferred design
options.misconception: believes a surviving underdrawing settles authorship, which it cannot do on its own

questions.explanation: A design that has to be transferred onto a panel cannot easily be altered once opaque colour is over it, so the composition is drawn first, often by pricking a full-size cartoon and rubbing charcoal or chalk through the holes, and the hand is free to correct the drawing itself. Only when the arrangement is settled does colour go on. The drawing therefore governs proportion, placement and the direction of every subsequent brushstroke, which is why a changed head or hand in the drawing corresponds to a changed picture. It is not a shading stage, since values are built in paint; it is not a warm layer, since that is what an imprimatura is; and it is not proof of hand, because the drawing may be by an assistant, a traced cartoon may come from another artist, and a skilled copyist can follow one closely.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions in a painting become expensive to reverse once colour is down.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: identify a sinopia and state what evidence it preserves
questions.stem: A wall painting has lost its colour layer, leaving a red-brown drawing of the figures lying directly on the plaster. What is that layer called, and what has it preserved?

options.text: A sinopia, an iron-oxide underdrawing that keeps the transferred cartoon and the design as first drawn
An imprimatura, the warm first coating that gives the finished picture its single unified tone
options.misconception: confuses a sinopia with an imprimatura, which belongs to panel and canvas practice

options.text: A bole, the red preparation brushed over gesso so that gold leaf laid on it would burnish
options.misconception: treats any red layer under a wall painting as bole, which is a gilding preparation

options.text: A secco passage, pigment bound in glue and laid onto the dry plaster, which is now coming away
options.misconception: reads a lost colour layer as a secco passage without checking what actually remains

questions.explanation: The word comes from the red earth used, sinopia being the Italian name for an iron-oxide clay. In fresco the wall is built in stages: a rough coat of plaster, then a sinopia drawn on that and left to dry, then the fresh intonaco laid over the drawing and painted into. Where the colour layer is lost, the sinopia is what survives, and it is unusually valuable because it is the design at its earliest state, before the painter committed to colour or adjusted a figure in the wet plaster. It therefore lets a restorer or scholar see the original cartoon, the transfer technique, and any point where the drawn figure and the painted figure differ. The alternatives are layers from other contexts: a bole under gold, an imprimatura under panel paint, and a secco passage is not a preparation at all but a detail added after drying.
questions.hint: Ask which stage of the wall's construction would leave a red drawing behind when the paint went.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a fresco wall is painted in daily sections
questions.learningObjective: explain the reason for the joins in a fresco wall
questions.stem: A wall painted in true fresco shows soft, slightly raised joins where one day's work met the next, and a thin line of loose grit runs along several of them. What causes this?

options.text: Each day's patch of wet plaster had to be laid and painted while it was workable, so the wall advanced a section at a time
Each day's underdrawing was brushed on a separate patch of the sinopia and pressed down by hand
options.misconception: calls the daily paint sections sinopie, which are the red preparatory drawings

options.text: A narrow level strip of plaster was left between the sections and filled in on the following day
options.misconception: confuses the float bridge joint with the whole of the daily working section

options.text: The painter lifted off each day's skin of plaster and re-laid it slightly out of true
options.misconception: confuses strappo removal of a wall with the sectioning of the wall in the first place

questions.explanation: True fresco is painted into fresh lime plaster, and the chemistry requires it: as the lime carbonates it grips whatever pigment is sitting in it, and the picture becomes part of the wall. But the plaster can only be worked while it is damp, so a large wall cannot be laid and painted at once. A patch the size of a day's labour, a giornata, is therefore filled and painted while it is still workable, and the next patch butts against it. The joins are the record of that rhythm: a slight ridge where one day's plaster overlapped the previous edge, and a line of grit where a float of plaster was used to weld the two sections together. The raised seam and the grit are thus evidence of the method, not of damage, and a restorer reads them as a map of the painter's working order.
questions.hint: Ask how long a patch of wet lime plaster stays workable, and what follows from the answer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why painting on dry plaster is less durable
questions.learningObjective: state the binder-level reason a secco passage is less durable
questions.stem: Details added to a wall after the plaster has dried are painted secco, in pigment bound with glue, wax or oil. Why are such passages usually the first to be lost?

options.text: The binder merely sits on the dry surface instead of becoming part of it, so nothing anchors the colour film
The dry plaster drinks the glue away, so no pigment can be held in place there at all
options.misconception: thinks the dry plaster absorbs the binder whole, when it takes the water and leaves the glue

options.text: Only earth pigments were used for such details, and those pigments were never lightfast
options.misconception: blames the pigment choice, which is a question of colour rather than of adhesion

options.text: The plaster was already finished when the detail was added, so the painter worked without a guide
options.misconception: explains a bonding failure by carelessness, ignoring the chemistry of the binder

questions.explanation: In buon fresco the pigment is trapped in the plaster's own structure as the lime carbonates, so the picture is fused to the wall and can only be lost with the wall. A secco passage has no such marriage: the pigment is suspended in a binder that dries as a film sitting on the surface, and the wall underneath is inert. That film is therefore always the weakest layer in the wall's construction, and it is exposed at once to handling, damp, salts drawn through the plaster, flaking, and the movement of the wall itself. Secco was used constantly and was not a failure, since it let a painter add blues, fine glazes and highlights that lime will not take, and much of it survives. The point is comparative rather than absolute: a secco passage is the part of the wall most likely to go first, and its loss is not a clue to the quality of the work.
questions.hint: Ask where the pigment ends up in each method, and which one is inside the wall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tempera panel was finished in oil
questions.learningObjective: explain why panel painters moved from tempera to oil glazes
questions.stem: Many fifteenth-century Italian panel paintings were begun in egg tempera and completed in oil glaze. What did the change of medium give the painter?

options.text: Transparent oil layers over a light tempera underpainting, so shadow could be deepened without becoming opaque
The ability to build a second layer at all, since tempera was said to be impossible to layer
options.misconception: believes tempera cannot be built up, though successive tempera coats are routine practice

options.text: A much longer working time, since egg yolk was said to set almost as soon as it was spread
options.misconception: confuses drying speed with layering; tempera dries fast but is still built up

options.text: A ground-free surface, since oil grips raw wood without any preparation beneath it
options.misconception: thinks oil skips the ground, when every technique needs one beneath it

questions.explanation: The two media behave differently in the same picture. Tempera dries fast, matte and light, which suits the job of laying in the forms with a light and a dark, and the pale underpainting it leaves is a good reflector for everything that follows. Oil, by contrast, dries slowly and stays transparent in a thin film, so a glaze of transparent colour laid over a light underlayer passes light down into it and comes back altered, which reads as depth. Working from a light tempera model and then glazing into it is what produced the luminous shadows and saturated colour of the period, and the two habits often sit side by side, with tempera continuing in the minute highlights where an oil glaze would be too slow. The change had nothing to do with a ban on layering, with drying time as such, or with any freedom from the ground.
questions.hint: Ask what a thin transparent film does to the light layer underneath it, and what that does to the colour.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a glaze produces depth of colour
questions.learningObjective: explain the optical effect of a transparent glaze
questions.stem: A painter builds a deep green drapery by laying a transparent green glaze over a pale underlayer instead of mixing a dark green pigment. What is the optical result?

options.text: The pale layer shows through the film, so the colour is lit from within and the surface looks deep
The two layers combine optically into one flat tone, exactly as two mixed pigments would
options.misconception: believes glazing is optically identical to mixing, which is why glazed passages differ

options.text: The film absorbs the light that would bounce back off the underlayer, so the result is merely darker
options.misconception: describes glazing as simple darkening and forgets the light returning from below

options.text: The film fills the ridges of the underpainting, so the passage becomes optically flatter and smoother
options.misconception: confuses glazing with a final levelling layer, which is a different operation

questions.explanation: A glaze is a layer thin enough to stay transparent, so light that enters it passes through to whatever is below and comes back out through the film again, coloured on the way out. What the eye then reports is a colour that is being generated inside the paint rather than reflected off its face, which is the ordinary meaning of depth in a picture. It also allows enormous subtlety: a green can be built by glazing one hue over another so that the mixture is never physically made on the palette, and a shadow can be deepened repeatedly without the colour going chalky or losing transparency. Two cautions follow. The layers are bound together, so stripping a glaze during cleaning can take the modelling with it and leave flat, light, dead colour. And because a glaze is transparent it also shows every flaw beneath it, including an uneven underpainting or an old fill.
questions.hint: Ask where the light goes after it enters the film, and what is below to send it back.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of an imprimatura on the finished picture
questions.stem: Before the main work, a prepared panel is often covered with a thin tinted stain called an imprimatura. What effect does that layer have on the finished picture?

options.text: It warms the light passages as they are built up, so its tone reads through the surface of the whole picture
It fixes the design to the panel by transfer, so the cartoon cannot shift while paint dries
options.misconception: confuses an imprimatura with the transferred drawing laid over the ground

options.text: It seals the panel against damp, taking over the work done by the glue size on bare wood
options.misconception: thinks the imprimatura is the barrier layer, when sizing is the barrier layer

options.text: It hardens the panel into a film, so the later paint layers cannot sink into the ground
options.misconception: believes the imprimatura is a hard seal rather than a thin transparent stain

questions.explanation: An imprimatura is deliberately weak. It is a transparent or near-transparent tint brushed over the ground, often a warm earth colour or a thin lead white, and its purpose is to establish a first value and a temperature for the whole picture so that the light areas will not come out cold. Because it is transparent, everything painted afterwards interacts with it, and the warmth survives in the lightest passages where the paint is thin, which is what makes a flesh passage look lit from within rather than filled in. Because it is thin it is also easy to see through in raking light, and a restorer can use its distribution to argue about how the picture was built. It does not carry the design, which is transferred separately, and it is not a seal, since that is the sizing's job beneath the ground.
questions.hint: Ask how opaque a warm stain needs to be in order to warm the lights that go on top of it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What sfumato changes in a face
questions.learningObjective: describe the effect of sfumato on the treatment of edges
questions.stem: Around the eyes and mouth of a sitter, the transitions between flesh tones are blended so that no edge is drawn anywhere. What is this softness usually called?

options.text: Sfumato, in which the contour dissolves into the surrounding tone and the form seems to emerge from shadow
Sfumato, in which the highlights are pushed brighter so that the face gains an artificial brilliance
options.misconception: thinks sfumato means heightened highlights rather than dissolved edges

options.text: Glazing, in which a final transparent film blurs the features and leaves the likeness deliberately uncertain
options.misconception: confuses the softening of edges with a glaze laid over the finished face

options.text: Glazing, in which no brown underpainting is allowed, so shadows must be mixed from flesh colour alone
options.misconception: thinks sfumato forbids underpainting, when it usually depends on it

questions.explanation: Sfumato names the loss of the contour, and the mechanism is cumulative: thin, semi-opaque films of lighter and darker paint are laid over a modelled underpainting, each one softening the edge of the last, until there is no line anywhere between the cheek and the shadow beside it. What the eye then gets is a form defined entirely by the slow change of tone, which is why the head appears to turn rather than to be outlined. It usually requires a substantial underpainting to work from, and it is expensive in time, which is part of why it is discussed as a difficulty rather than a manner. It is not a matter of brighter highlights, since a highlight needs an edge to be bright against, and it is not a transparent coating laid over a finished face, which would sit on the surface instead of merging with the flesh beneath.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the line where a face meets the background, and to the line where two flesh tones meet.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pentimento evidences
questions.learningObjective: state what a changed outline beneath the paint proves
questions.stem: In a portrait a faint outline of a broad hat shows through the paint, and it does not match the headgear the sitter actually wears. What does that ghost image establish?

options.text: That the composition was changed while the picture was in progress, so the visible design is not the first one
That two different hands worked on the panel, since a ghost outline cannot come from one painter
options.misconception: reads every pentimento as proof of a second hand, which is not what it shows

options.text: That the varnish has darkened unevenly, leaving a paler halo where the hat once was
options.misconception: confuses an alteration in the paint with a discoloration in the varnish

options.text: That the panel was reused from an older picture whose composition was never scraped away
options.misconception: jumps to a reused support without first examining the paint layers

questions.explanation: A pentimento is the record of a decision that was taken back. The painter blocked in one shape, and then painted over it, and the earlier shape survives because the first layer is thicker, less even, or differently coloured than the paint that buried it, so light and infrared examination still separate the two. What it evidences is narrow and useful: the composition stood at a different point, and the change was made by someone working on the picture, at a time when the paint was still workable. It does not follow that there were two painters, since a single hand alters a design as often as it fixes one. Nor does it point to a varnish problem, to a reused support, or to an old composition beneath, since those would leave evidence elsewhere. Pentimenti are the ordinary condition of a painting in progress, and they are among the clearest windows into how a picture was arrived at.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true of the first layer for its outline to still be readable under the second.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: read a craquelure pattern as evidence about the support
questions.stem: A panel painting shows fine cracks that follow the grain of the wood and run across the paint layers, opened slightly and darkened with dirt. What does that pattern point to?

options.text: Long movement of the wooden support, since a stiff paint film cannot stretch as the panel swells and shrinks
One sudden blow to the front, since an impact opens cracks that radiate from the point of contact
options.misconception: reads any crack network as impact damage, ignoring the grain-following regularity

options.text: Paint that was mixed badly, since a weak film cracks as soon as it has dried
options.misconception: blames the paint mixture, when a grain-following network points to the support

options.text: A recent varnish, since a drying film shrinks and pulls the paint into a crackle of its own
options.misconception: believes varnish creates the network rather than filling and darkening an existing one

questions.explanation: Wood is hygroscopic. It takes up moisture when the air is damp and gives it up when it is dry, and it does so most across the grain, so a panel changes width by a fraction of a millimetre several times a year. The paint films on top are far more rigid than the wood and cannot follow that movement, so they fail in tension and open a network of cracks whose direction is set by the structure beneath them, which is why the lines run with the grain and cross the paint layers. Over decades the cracks admit dirt and hold it, so the network darkens, and the panel may then be cradled from behind to limit further movement. Impact damage looks different, being local and radiating, and a varnish is not the source of the network, though a discoloured varnish can make an old one look recent.
questions.hint: Ask what a wooden panel does across the grain when the humidity of the room changes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: interpret fluorescence as evidence of a later varnish layer
questions.stem: Under ultraviolet light a broad haze of fluorescence covers the whole surface of a picture, and it is brightest where the painting is darkest. What does the haze most likely represent?

options.text: A varnish applied long after the painting, which has yellowed and deepened the colours beneath it
Retouching in modern paint, which always behaves differently from the original colour layers
options.misconception: reads the fluorescence as retouching rather than as a varnish film over it

options.text: The original chalk ground, which shines under ultraviolet light because of its gypsum content
options.misconception: thinks ground fluoresces like varnish, confusing a fill material with a coating

options.text: Water staining from an old flood, which leaves a bright residue inside the paint film
options.misconception: assumes any fluorescence is water damage without locating it in a single layer

questions.explanation: A natural resin varnish oxidises and yellows as it ages, and old varnishes fluoresce under ultraviolet light, so an even haze across the whole surface is the standard sign of a coating that is not the artist's own final layer. The darker areas glow most because the varnish is thickest in proportion to the amount of light the paint beneath absorbs, which is why the shadows and the deep colours look muffled and brown while the lights look comparatively fresh. That dulling has a cost: the colours the painter mixed are no longer the colours now on the wall, so a cleaning and re-varnishing is often proposed and must be argued for on the ground that the varnish is doing damage. The fluorescence has to be read alongside the layers themselves, because retouching, an old fill and water residue can also fluoresce, but they are local rather than uniform.
questions.hint: Ask why the deepest shadows are the places where a coating shows up most strongly.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a canvas support changes the drawing
questions.learningObjective: compare the drawn line on canvas and on panel
questions.stem: A painter moves from a rigid gessoed panel to a stretched linen canvas and repeats the same drawing. What difference does the support make to the line?

options.text: The woven ground flexes and catches a firm line, so contours tend to be broader, softer and broken
The weave offers no tooth at all, so lines can be drawn as fine and sharp as on a gessoed panel
options.misconception: thinks canvas is smoother than panel, ignoring the pronounced relief of the weave

options.text: The fabric stretches permanently, so a drawn line stays distorted once the tacking is loosened
options.misconception: believes the line is permanently distorted, when slack causes this and tightening undoes it

options.text: Only wood accepts a drawing under the paint, so on canvas the design has to be painted straight in
options.misconception: thinks only panel takes an underdrawing, which is not true of either support

questions.explanation: A tightly stretched linen surface is not flat in the way a gessoed panel is. The weave stands slightly proud in one direction and hollow in the other, so a hard chalk or charcoal line laid across it catches on the crowns and skips in the hollows, and the line that results is soft, broken and slightly scattered. A painter works with that, since an oil or tempera line drawn in rather than rubbed on will read strongly, and the broader, more searching contours typical of canvas are partly a response to what the support will accept. Canvas is not smooth, and it does not forbid underdrawing, for a transferred design or a charcoal layout works on it as well as on wood. And the distortion of a drawing is a function of slack, not of the material: a canvas allowed to hang loose will deform, and re-tensioning it puts the drawing back.
questions.hint: Ask what a hard chalk line does as it crosses the raised and hollow parts of a woven cloth.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a triptych's wings were for
questions.learningObjective: state the function of the hinged wings of a triptych
questions.stem: A triptych has a fixed central panel and two side panels joined to it by working hinges. In its ordinary use, what do the two wings do?

options.text: They fold shut over the centre, so the work can be closed, protected from handling and carried
They stand open to widen the scene, so that more figures can be fitted into the narrative
options.misconception: thinks the wings only ever open, ignoring that closed is their commonest position

options.text: They carry a fixed inscription naming the donors, which had to remain visible at all times
options.misconception: believes the wings exist for text, when inscriptions belong to the fixed frame

options.text: They hold a separate stretched canvas that was displayed across the front of the work
options.misconception: invents a function for the wings that no construction of the object supports

questions.explanation: The hinges make the wings movable, and a movable wing is only worth the trouble of building if there is a position it is normally not in. Closed is that position: the two wings meet at the centre and cover the principal scene, which protects a surface that would otherwise take every stray hand and every change of light, and it turns a three-panel object into a single package that can be carried, stored, and locked. Shown, the wings are given over to other subjects, usually announced on their outer faces when closed, so that the closed and open readings are two different pictures rather than one picture with spare parts. Inscriptions naming donors belong to the fixed frame, which is where they stay visible in either position, and no stretched canvas is involved in the construction of a hinged altarpiece.
questions.hint: Ask what a hinged panel is for if the picture is only ever seen with it open.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial logic of an altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: explain how the tiers of an altarpiece order the image
questions.stem: A large altarpiece is built as a carved framework divided into tiers, with the main scene across the centre and smaller compartments above it. What does the tiering do?

options.text: It grades the figures by height, so an upper tier reads as raised and closer than the main panel below
It flattens everything onto one plane, so the compartments deliberately prevent any depth at all
options.misconception: reads the tiers as a refusal of depth rather than as a device that makes it

options.text: It conceals the carved frame, so the whole is read as an unframed wall painting of one piece
options.misconception: believes the frame is hidden, when carved framing is a principal part of the work

options.text: It merges the scenes into one continuous action, so the tiers are only practical carpentry
options.misconception: ignores the spatial hierarchy the tiers create in favour of the joinery

questions.explanation: An altarpiece is a piece of furniture as well as a picture, and its frame is a set of shelves for images. Tiering is the cheapest way to build a hierarchy out of flat panels: put a half-length figure at eye level in the centre, and something smaller in a compartment set higher, and the eye reads the higher one as raised above, and therefore nearer to, the space of the viewer, while the low wide panel is read as a stage further off. The same logic lets a sculptor work larger than life in the upper tiers without breaking scale with the principal scene below. It does not flatten the image, since the tiers are precisely a way of making it deep without a single coherent floor; it does not hide the frame, which is one of the most carved parts of the object; and the compartments are doing the reading, not the carpentry.
questions.hint: Ask why a small figure in a high compartment does not read as a distant figure.

questions.stem: Beneath the main panels of an altarpiece runs a low strip of small scenes inside its own continuous moulding. What is the strip called, and what does it add?

options.text: The predella, which carries a run of episodes telling the story the main panel only begins
The dado, a plain moulded base fitted to keep the altarpiece clear of the church floor
options.misconception: confuses the predella with an architectural base that carries no narrative

options.text: The entablature, an overhanging cornice fitted to spread the weight of the frame above
options.misconception: confuses the predella with a cornice, which sits above the frame rather than below

options.text: The antependium, a painted cloth that hung in front of the altar and told the same story
options.misconception: treats a fixed part of the frame as a hanging altarcloth

questions.explanation: A predella is the row of small narrative panels beneath the main compartment of an altarpiece, and it does the job the tall panel cannot. A single large figure, often standing and often filling the height of the frame, has no room for a plot: the painter can give it presence, scale and dignity, but not a sequence of events. The predella, with a long horizontal format and a series of separate scenes, supplies the sequence, and it does so close to the level of the worshipper and to the altar table, where it can be read while the main panel above is contemplated as an image. The strip is a fixed part of the frame, not a cloth, not a plain base and not a cornice, and its moulding usually continues the frame's own profile so that the whole reads as one object.
questions.hint: Ask where in the format a sequence of separate episodes can fit, and where a single large figure fits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The convention behind a sacra conversazione
questions.learningObjective: state the convention that governs a sacra conversazione
questions.stem: The Virgin and Child are seated among saints drawn from different centuries, gathered in a single space and lit by one light. What convention is this, and what does it assume?

options.text: Sacra conversazione, which sets figures of different ages together as if in one company at one moment
A chronicle arrangement, which lists the saints in the order in which the church received them
options.misconception: assumes the sequence is documentary, when the grouping is a pictorial convention

options.text: A celestial hierarchy, which ranks the figures by the feast on which each is celebrated
options.misconception: reads a grouped company as a ranking rather than as a gathering

options.text: A narrative sequence, in which the figures appear in the order of one evening's events
options.misconception: treats a static grouping as a series of successive actions

questions.explanation: The convention is deliberate anachronism. Saints who lived centuries apart are placed in one room, sharing a floor, a light and a scale, and the resulting picture is not a scene that happened but a statement about their company. The altarpiece had to hold figures whom a viewer might recognise by attribute, and putting them together in one setting made them simultaneously present to the worshipper and to the altar, which is the devotional point of the arrangement. Nothing in the picture depends on chronology or on feast order, and nothing in it records a sequence of actions, since the figures are seated and conversing rather than acting. The single light and the shared space are what make the group read as one company, and it is those, not the identity of the figures, that the convention is designed to produce.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer is meant to conclude about figures who could not have met in life.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The constraint that shaped the icon
questions.learningObjective: identify the practical constraint behind icon uniformity
questions.stem: Byzantine icons follow set formulas for the face, the eyes and the modelling, so that two icons of the same subject look closely alike. What chiefly produced that uniformity?

options.text: That the panel had to be small, portable and read closely, so a few set features stayed legible at a glance
That pigment was scarce, so the palette was restricted to a few cheap earth colours
options.misconception: blames the uniformity on pigment supply, which is not what constrains the face

options.text: That the church forbade any new invention in the human figure on any date at all
options.misconception: assumes a flat prohibition rather than a practical and devotional rule

options.text: That the panel had to be completed in a single sitting, so one method was used throughout
options.misconception: ties the formulas to the length of the working day, which they do not follow from

questions.explanation: An icon is not a portrait hung in a gallery. It is a portable panel, often of a size suited to being held or set into a small frame, carried in procession, kissed, and placed close to the eye, and it has to work at that scale and in candlelight. A face modelled with soft naturalistic transitions loses its features at small size and in a low light, whereas a long nose, a strong line of the brows, a small mouth and sharp highlights in the shadow survive, and the same set of formulas is the reliable way to guarantee the survival. That the formulas are reproducible also matters, since an icon had to be recognisably the same icon. The reasons people usually give, pigment scarcity, a blanket ban on invention, and the time available in one sitting, do not account for the specificity of the features or for the reliance on a small legible panel.
questions.hint: Ask what the icon has to be able to do at the size and the light in which it is normally seen.

questions.topic: What an iconostasis is
questions.learningObjective: identify an iconostasis and state its structural role
questions.stem: A low screen of carved, gilded and painted panels, arranged in tiers and standing across a church, separates the sanctuary from the nave. What is this screen?

options.text: An iconostasis, a screen of icons marking the boundary of the sanctuary in the Eastern rite
A rood screen, whose upper panels carry the painted stations of the cross in the Western rite
options.misconception: confuses an iconostasis with a Western rood screen, which serves a different rite

options.text: A templon, the marble barrier on which the altar stood in the earliest churches of the tradition
options.misconception: confuses the screen of icons with the sanctuary parapet of earlier church plans

options.text: A choir screen, fitted between the stalls to separate the singing clergy from the congregation
options.misconception: confuses the icon screen with the choir furniture standing near it

questions.explanation: An iconostasis is the screen that closes off the sanctuary in the Eastern Christian churches, and it is built of images rather than of openwork alone. Tiered arrangements carry rows of icons, the lowest tier standing on the floor and the highest below the vault, with a central set of doors standing open so the celebrant can be seen, and the whole thing is a theological statement about the wall between the seen and the unseen as well as a practical barrier. The rood screen is a different object from a different tradition, carrying the cross and often the stations, and it belongs to Latin churches. A templon is the low parapet found in early plans, and choir screens are furniture placed near the sanctuary rather than the boundary itself. What identifies the object is the icons and the rite, not the carving.
questions.hint: Ask what a screen in this tradition is carrying, and which rite uses it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the height of the vanishing point does
questions.learningObjective: explain why the vanishing point is placed at the viewer's eye level
questions.stem: In a one-point construction the orthogonals of a receding pavement meet at a single point, and that point is painted at the height of the viewer's own eye. Why is it placed there?

options.text: So that the painted space and the real space share one eye level, which is what makes the floor read as continuous
So that the horizon sits in the upper third, a proportion the eye finds restful in a balanced composition
options.misconception: treats the eye-level placement as a compositional preference rather than a physical match

options.text: So that the picture can be hung without a frame and still show a level horizon to the room it hangs in
options.misconception: believes the placement is a way of levelling the wall, which the frame already does

options.text: So that the point can be struck with a single pair of compasses from any two of the orthogonals
options.misconception: confuses a drafting convenience with the reason for the height of the point

questions.explanation: A painting is not a window, but this is the convention that makes it work like one. Every line drawn parallel to the picture's surface, in the real world, appears to converge at a point as far away as the eye can follow it, and that point always lies on the horizon, which is the height at which the eye is held. A viewer looking at a picture naturally looks from about the height of their own body, so if the painted horizon is set at that same height the two match and the painted floor seems to run away from the viewer's feet rather than float in front of them. Move the horizon much higher in the picture and the viewer is looking down on the scene from above, which is the source of the bird's-eye effect. A pleasing proportion is a real consideration in placing a horizon, but it is not what fixes its height.
questions.hint: Ask where a real horizon appears when you stand in a room and look level across it.

questions.topic: What a reflected window does in a mirror picture
questions.learningObjective: state the self-reference made by a reflection that includes the viewer
questions.stem: In a picture of a darkened room, a window is reflected in a convex mirror at the back, and the reflection contains a small figure standing in the space in front of the picture. What is the painting doing?

options.text: It locates the viewer inside the room, so the picture asserts that it is being looked at by someone standing there
It certifies the interior, since the reflected detail shows the room was measured rather than invented
options.misconception: reads a reflection as documentary proof, when a picture can reflect anything it likes

options.text: It enlarges the interior, since a mirror on the back wall doubles the space beyond the picture
options.misconception: believes the mirror adds real space, forgetting that the glass is inside the image

options.text: It fixes the hour, since the light coming through the one window sets the time of the scene
options.misconception: reads the window as a lighting note rather than as a claim about the viewer

questions.explanation: A convex mirror has a wide field of view, so it can gather into a small disc the whole of the room in front of it, including the wall the picture hangs on. Put a reflection of the viewer into that disc and the picture stops being a window onto somewhere else and becomes an object that knows it is being watched. The device is not primarily documentary: a painter invents the reflected interior as freely as the rest, so the reflection certifies nothing about a real room. Nor does it enlarge anything, since the glass is painted and stays inside the image, and the window is a light source like any other rather than a statement about time. What it changes is the picture's claim about itself, and about the body standing in front of it.
questions.hint: Ask what a convex mirror can see that a flat mirror cannot, and who is standing where.

questions.topic: The claim made by a trompe l'oeil
questions.learningObjective: state the claim a trompe l'oeil makes about its own objects
questions.stem: A painted curtain hangs from a painted nail, a painted shadow falls on the wall behind it, and a painted stone ledge runs in front of both. What is this picture claiming?

options.text: That the objects are present at the picture's surface, so the wall behind them becomes the wall of the room
That the objects are permanently out of reach, since paint cannot cross the plane of the picture
options.misconception: assumes the illusion concedes the flat surface, which is exactly what it denies

options.text: That the room is a stage, so the curtain is scenery standing in front of a painted backdrop
options.misconception: takes a painted curtain for a real one, confusing the fiction with the device

options.text: That the light in the picture agrees with the real light of the room the picture now hangs in
options.misconception: reads the illusion as an exercise in lighting rather than in deceptive appearance

questions.explanation: Trompe l'oeil works by borrowing the ordinary conditions under which a painted object is believed. The object has to cast a shadow, because objects cast shadows. It has to be attached to something, so the nail is painted. It has to be behind the ledge and in front of the wall, so a consistent order of overlaps is established, with a cast shadow marking the gap between curtain and wall. Once all of that is in place the eye makes the ordinary inference and locates the curtain in the room rather than on the panel, and the wall behind it becomes the wall the picture hangs on. The claim is deliberately and falsely complete, which is why these pictures depend on frames, ledges, grilles and a real doorframe to cover the joints where one kind of space gives way to the other.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye needs to see before it will believe a painted curtain is hanging in the room.

questions.topic: The viewpoint an anamorphosis requires
questions.learningObjective: state the viewing position an anamorphosis depends on
questions.stem: A painted image spread across a curved surface looks like an incoherent smear when seen head-on and resolves into a recognisable figure from one point in the room. What does that demand of a viewer?

options.text: That they stand at one narrow point off the axis, since the picture only resolves from the position it was worked out for
That they walk right around the surface, since the image resolves equally well from every side of it
options.misconception: assumes the distortion is uniform, ignoring that the projection fixes one viewpoint

options.text: That they use a mirror to undo the distortion, since the curve is a fault in the image itself
options.misconception: thinks a mirror is part of the device, when the resolution happens directly by eye

options.text: That they look at the surface square on, since distortion only appears when it is seen head-on
options.misconception: reverses the arrangement, putting the resolvable view at right angles

questions.explanation: An anamorphosis is a picture drawn for one eye in one place. The image is deliberately stretched along the direction of curvature, so that from the intended station the foreshortening of the surface exactly cancels the stretching, and the marks reassemble into a whole figure. Move a step and the cancellation fails: the picture becomes a smear again. That is not a defect, because the piece is designed as a collaboration between a surface and a position, and the audience has to find the position, usually by moving about, which turns looking into a task the viewer performs rather than something handed to them. This is why such works are almost always placed in a corridor or a recess where the approach is narrow, and why the single correct view is the point of the object rather than an accident of it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the stretched marks when the eye leaves the point the picture was made for.

questions.topic: What a still life can carry beyond likeness
questions.learningObjective: state the symbolic content a still life arrangement can carry
questions.stem: A still life shows a cracked clay jug, a loaf broken open and a flowering branch laid on a stone ledge against a dark ground. What can such a picture carry besides likeness?

options.text: A reading in which the vessel stands for the body and its uses, so the arrangement becomes a statement about mortality
A record of the market stall the objects came from, since such pictures were painted from goods on sale
options.misconception: treats the arrangement as a document of shopping rather than a constructed theme

options.text: A display of the painter's handling, which was the single thing a buyer of a still life asked for
options.misconception: reduces the genre to virtuosity and denies the symbolic content entirely

options.text: A household instruction, since pictures of food and vessels hung in kitchens as a teaching text
options.misconception: assumes a didactic domestic function that the pictures are not recorded as having

questions.explanation: A still life is an arrangement, not a snapshot. The painter chooses which vessel, in what condition, holding what, and sets it at a particular angle to the light, and every one of those choices carries meaning that the object would not carry in a kitchen. Cracks, bites taken out of the fruit, fallen petals and stems that will not hold all point the same way: things are beautiful and they are used up. Because the jug and the loaf stand for the body and for the life it sustains, the still life can carry a serious claim about mortality within the exacting conventions of a genre otherwise devoted to texture and light. The shopping, the pure display of skill and the domestic teaching text are all reductions of that, and each of them leaves the arrangement's chosen condition unexplained.
questions.hint: Ask why the painter chose a cracked jug and a broken loaf rather than intact ones.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Which objects signal a vanitas
questions.learningObjective: identify the objects that declare the theme of a vanitas
questions.stem: A still life includes a snuffed candle, a running hourglass, a skull, a flower past its bloom and a single coin. What is this picture declaring?

options.text: That time, wealth and beauty all pass and end, with each object naming one way in which they do
That the table it records was laid for a banquet, since these were the dishes served at one
options.misconception: reads the objects as a record of a meal, ignoring the declared theme

options.text: That a young life is brief, with the fading flower standing for the flowering of a body
options.misconception: confines the reading to the flower and discards the rest of the group

options.text: That the bones were studied from life, since the skull is a record of their structure
options.misconception: reads a symbol as an anatomical study, which is a different kind of picture

questions.explanation: The vanitas assembles objects that each stand for a limited thing and then name its ending. The snuffed candle and the running hourglass measure time and show it spent. The coin stands for money, and money is spent too. The flower past its bloom stands for beauty and the body's short season, and the skull, which outlives everything else in the picture, stands for the destination. The theme is only complete because all of them are present: take away the coin and the statement is narrower, take away the skull and it is about transience rather than death. That is why a vanitas is arranged as a composition of separate significations rather than as a scene, and why the objects are shown in perfect, still, silent isolation instead of being used by anyone.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity each object is there to measure, and what each of them then shows running out.

questions.topic: The hierarchy inside a history painting
questions.learningObjective: explain how height, centrality and light rank figures in a history painting
questions.stem: In a large history painting a central figure stands full length and lit, while attendants and defeated enemies are set lower, bent and in shadow. What is at work in the arrangement?

options.text: A hierarchy of importance, with height, centrality and light used to rank the figures by their significance
A rule of perspective, with the upright figure necessarily the one standing nearest the picture plane
options.misconception: attributes the placement to distance, when height and centrality carry the meaning

options.text: A record of working order, with the shadowed figures being the ones the painter finished last
options.misconception: reads darkness as a note about the working method rather than about significance

options.text: A rule of costume, with each figure placed according to the era of the clothes being worn
options.misconception: thinks placement follows costume, ignoring the compositional ranking entirely

questions.explanation: History painting was the genre that carried the highest claim because it was thought to require the most learning: a story, a knowledge of the antique, a command of many figures and a hierarchy of expression. Within it, importance is staged spatially. Whoever matters is put upright in the light and near the centre, and whoever matters less is bent, turned, in profile, compressed and in shadow, so that the eye arrives at the significant figure first and reads the others as the setting it happens in. This is a convention, not a law, and painters break it deliberately to shock. It is not perspective, since nothing about distance requires a figure to stand up. Nor does it record who was painted last or what anyone was wearing, both of which are facts about the workshop rather than the story.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye reaches first in the picture, and what the arrangement of the others is for.

questions.topic: The convention that makes a landscape legible
questions.learningObjective: explain how repoussoir and aerial perspective order a landscape
questions.stem: A landscape sets a dark mass of trees and rock against one edge in the near foreground, and carries the middle distance through paler and cooler tones to a low far horizon. What is this arrangement doing?

options.text: It sets a dark repoussoir at the front to push the view back, and uses aerial perspective to make distance recede
It records the weather of the day, since the pale tones stand for mist lying in the valley
options.misconception: reads the tonal gradient as a meteorological report rather than a depth device

options.text: It maps the estate, since the bands of land stand for the fields the patron actually owned
options.misconception: believes the landscape is a cadastral record, which the arrangement does not claim

options.text: It follows the frame, since a dark mass at one edge is what the carved moulding of a panel supplies
options.misconception: derives the repoussoir from the frame instead of from the composition

questions.explanation: A dark, sharply drawn mass at the front of a landscape does the work of a closed hand held up in front of the eye: it gives an immediate near thing, and having been given, the middle distance must be further. Everything then falls away from it in graded steps. Contrast of handling does as much work as contrast of tone, since a near tree is described with separate, loaded strokes and a far hill is a thin wash of nearly the colour of the sky. That fading of contrast and of saturation with distance is aerial perspective, and it is a convention in the sense that it is a systematic device for ordering a flat field, not a report of any particular day's weather. The device is unrelated to the carved frame, and reading a landscape as a map of ownership mistakes a picture for a document.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye needs in front of it before it will accept that the space goes back a long way.

questions.topic: What a capriccio is
questions.learningObjective: identify a capriccio by its invented architecture
questions.stem: A picture combines a monumental arch, a broken column and a distant tower in one setting, a combination the artist had never seen built and never could have seen built. What is this kind of picture?

options.text: A capriccio, an invented architectural fantasy assembled out of known forms for the sake of the design
A veduta, a view recorded on the spot and valued precisely for its correspondence to a real place
options.misconception: confuses an invented view with a recorded one, which is the whole difference here

options.text: A record of a composite scheme, drawn for a patron who had commissioned all of the buildings shown
options.misconception: assumes the ensemble existed, which is precisely what the picture denies

options.text: A ceiling illusion, in which the architecture is painted overhead to make a small room look larger
options.misconception: confuses invented architecture with overhead illusionism, which is a different problem

questions.explanation: A capriccio is architecture that was never built, and its subject is the pleasure of the assembly rather than any place. The painter takes forms already known, an arch from one source, a column from another, a tower from a third, sometimes including fragments that cannot be stood in at all, and sets them together at a scale and in a light that make the combination read as a real city. Because the ensemble is invented it can be arranged to serve the composition, so the arch frames the view and the tower closes it, which is exactly the freedom a recorded view does not offer. A veduta is the opposite case, prized for matching the place, and an overhead illusion is solving a different problem with the same materials. The category is a matter of what the picture claims, not of what is in it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the buildings in the picture were ever standing in that arrangement.

questions.topic: What a nocturne requires
questions.learningObjective: state what a nocturne has to invent in order to be painted
questions.stem: A street is painted after dark, lit by a single lantern and a shaft of moonlight, with most of the canvas sunk in deep brown. What does such a picture have to supply?

options.text: A light worked out entirely in the paint, since almost no usable light reaches the sheet at that hour
A quicker and thinner paint layer throughout, since darkness is achieved by leaving the ground bare
options.misconception: assumes darkness is made by absence, when it must still be modelled paint

options.text: A much larger support, since a night scene has to be read from further away than a day one
options.misconception: ties the scale of the support to the subject, which it does not follow from

options.text: The abandonment of underdrawing, since a linear construction would be lost in so little light
options.misconception: supposes the absence of visible light removes the need for a construction

questions.explanation: A nocturne is one of the few subjects in which the painter has almost nothing to look at. Outdoors after dark, forms are legible only where a lamp, a moon or a lit window reaches them, and everything else is a mass of uncertainty. The picture therefore has to be built from a light source that exists on the canvas, and the whole structure follows from where that source is placed and how far it reaches. That is a real constraint and not a stylistic whim: the lantern has to model the forms beside it, throw a shadow in a consistent direction, and die away at a plausible distance, while the surrounding darkness has to be a built brown that still carries shapes rather than a bare support. The scale of the support and the use of underdrawing are separate decisions that the hour does not dictate.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the real scene the painter can actually see, and where the light has to come from.

questions.topic: A pricked cartoon under finished paint
questions.learningObjective: read a transferred cartoon as evidence of the working order
questions.stem: A panel is examined in infrared light. Dotted pricking lines from a full-size cartoon run through the whole figure, including a set of drapery folds across the shoulder that appear nowhere in the paint. What does the examination show?

options.text: That the design was pricked out in full beforehand, and the drapery was then rearranged once the paint was on
That the panel carries a transferred engraving, so the dotted lines are hatching from a print
options.misconception: reads a pricked cartoon as a print transfer, which leaves a different trace

options.text: That the panel is a modello, and the dotted lines belong to a larger study of the same design
options.misconception: assumes a small preliminary version, when the dotted lines record the actual support

options.text: That the panel has been lined, so the dotted lines sit on a canvas beneath the wood
options.misconception: confuses a drawing showing through with a second support under the panel

questions.explanation: The pricking is the mechanism of the transfer. Holes were pricked along the cartoon's lines, the cartoon laid on the ground, and charcoal or chalk dusted through, so a continuous dotted line appears exactly where the design ran. Its presence across the whole figure shows that the composition was set out completely before colour, and its disagreement with the paint shows that the paint departed from it. A fold drawn and not painted is a pentimento of the ordinary kind: the shoulder was rearranged once the modelling was under way, and the transfer is what preserves the discarded alternative. The trace is not a print, which would leave a reversed hatched image, and not a modello, which would be a second object. It is the record of a decision taken back on this panel.
questions.hint: Ask how a full-size design gets from the cartoon onto the ground, and what is left behind.

questions.topic: Graded handling in a landscape
questions.learningObjective: read contrast of handling as a depth device
questions.stem: A landscape's near hillside is built from thick, sharp-edged strokes of brown and green, while the plain and river behind are thin, pale and blurred, and the far hills are almost the colour of the sky. What is the painter doing?

Recording two working methods, with the near hill painted wet and the far hills painted quite dry
options.misconception: reads a graded distance as a note about the order of execution

options.text: Recording a change of weather, since the far hills stand in mist and the near hill does not
options.misconception: takes a pictorial device as a report of the day's conditions

options.text: Copying a print source, since prints are normally graded from a dark foreground to a pale distance
options.misconception: assumes a printed source, where the grading is a choice of the painter

Stacking these contrasts from the front of the picture to the back is a systematic way of composing distance, and it works even in a monochrome print, where tone alone would have to carry the whole burden. What it records is not the order in which the painter worked, since a distant passage can be laid in first, nor the weather, though mist is a convenient excuse for a pale band, and it has nothing to do with having a print in front of the painter.
questions.hint: Ask what an edge can tell the eye that a tone alone cannot.

questions.topic: The condition of the objects in a still life
questions.learningObjective: read the condition of depicted objects as a symbolic choice
questions.stem: A still life is set on a stone ledge against a dark ground: a lemon halved with its cut face turned out, a cracked wine glass, and a bunch of grapes with several berries fallen and bruised. What is the viewer invited to read?

options.text: Signs of use and of time passing, so the arrangement carries a sense of the body's own fragility
A record of the household's diet, since the fruit sets out what the family could afford to eat
options.misconception: reads the arrangement as a social document and misses the symbolic content

options.text: A comparison of textures, with fruit, glass and stone set to display the painter's handling
options.misconception: reduces the picture to technique, which does not explain the chosen conditions

options.text: A warning about dishonesty, since the fallen fruit stands for goods taken without payment
options.misconception: attaches a moral to the fruit that the arrangement does not state

questions.explanation: Nothing in a still life is in a condition by accident. A half lemon turned cut-face out, a glass already cracked, fruit on the ledge rather than in the bowl: these are choices, and they are choices that point the same way, toward use, consumption and the short reach of a body's freshness. The tradition in which such a picture sits was developed by painters who could make the objects beautiful, so the point of the decay is not ugliness but the fact that the beautiful thing is passing. The arrangement is therefore not a menu, a technical exercise or a moral allegory about theft, although a viewer may add meanings of that kind. What it declares is a coincidence between the transience of fruit and the transience of the body it stands for.
questions.hint: Ask why the painter chose to show a cracked glass and a bruised berry rather than sound ones.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Status signals in a portrait
questions.learningObjective: identify the attributes that signal standing in a portrait
questions.stem: A portrait shows the sitter standing in a walled garden, one gloved hand on a stone parapet, a book and a folded letter on the ledge, a small badge at the shoulder, and a long gown rather than working dress. What is it communicating?

options.text: Learning, lineage and gentle standing, assembled from the objects, the badge and the dress that signal them
The sitter's trade, since the parapet and the garden are the tools of the work being shown
options.misconception: reads the setting as an occupational record, which the objects do not claim

options.text: Wealth alone, since each object in the picture is entered at the price it would have cost
options.misconception: reduces every attribute to a purchase price and misses what they denote

options.text: Piety, since the book and the letter are both devotional texts placed for devotion
options.misconception: assumes a religious reading that the objects support only weakly

questions.explanation: A portrait of this kind is a set of assertions built out of things a viewer already knows how to read. A book says the sitter is literate and leisured enough to read; a letter says there is correspondence, a business of the world, someone to write to; a small badge or device ties the sitter to a family or a house; gloves and a long gown say that the hands of this person do not work and that the person stands in a rank. The parapet and the garden set a leisure outside the household business. None of this is a price list, though the objects do imply means, and none of it is a record of a trade, since the parapet is not a tool. The reading is cumulative and conventional, and each attribute answers a different question about who the sitter is.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer already knows from seeing a book, a badge and a pair of gloves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Lamplight on water in a nocturne
questions.learningObjective: interpret the treatment of reflected light in a night scene
questions.stem: A canal at night shows a boat crossing a pool of lamplight, a bridge in near silhouette, and the reflection pulled down the water in long vertical strokes. What is the painter solving?

options.text: How to make an invented light behave as a real one on the moving water as well as on the built forms
How to record the actual darkness of the hour, since no detail would have been visible at all
options.misconception: reads the scene as a claim about visibility rather than about constructed light

options.text: How to keep the composition legible, since the vertical strokes stand in for a lost construction
options.misconception: treats the reflections as a substitute for a linear scheme, which they are not

options.text: How to show the current in the canal, since the strokes are records of the water's movement
options.misconception: confuses a device for depicting a light with a device for depicting a current

questions.explanation: A reflection on moving water is governed by a rule the eye knows and the painter has to obey. A bright source at a distance in a level plane does not come back as a small sharp image, which is what a flat mirror would give; it comes back as a long broken column running towards the viewer, broken because the surface tilts this way and that, and dimmer as it comes forward. Painting that column is what makes the water read as water and the lamp as a lamp, and getting it wrong flattens the canal into a sheet of brown with a bright spot on it. The strokes are therefore a light described under a known optical rule. They are not a record of the actual darkness, of the current, nor a replacement for a drawn structure, and the boat has to be lit from the same invented source as everything else.
questions.hint: Ask what a light in a level plane looks like when it comes back off a rippled surface towards you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The outer faces of a triptych
questions.learningObjective: explain why the closed faces of a triptych are painted in grisaille
questions.stem: An altarpiece is examined with its wings shut. The two outer faces carry a standing figure in grey, painted to look like carved and gilded wood, and no colour. Why is this arrangement informative?

options.text: The grisaille imitates carving, so the closed object reads as a shrine rather than as two painted scenes
Colour was beyond the workshop, so the wings were left at the underpainting stage by necessity
options.misconception: explains a deliberate convention as a shortage, which the finishing shows it is not

options.text: The outer faces were later stripped, and the monochrome is what survives of an old cleaning
options.misconception: assumes a later loss, where the monochrome is a finished and intended surface

options.text: The wings were meant to stay open, so the closed state is a storage condition rather than a view
options.misconception: denies the closed position, which is the state the grisaille was painted for

questions.explanation: When the wings are shut, the closed faces are what the object presents to the rest of the church, and often what it presents when it is carried or stored. Painting them in grisaille, in shades of grey and brown arranged to look like sculpture under a raking light, is a way of making the closed object read as what it also physically is: a panelled and carved shrine, with a figure in relief on either side. The convention makes the two states cohere, since the painted carving in grey and the real carved gilt frame belong to the same world. It is a finished surface rather than an abandoned or stripped one, since the shading is deliberate and the seams are concealed. And the closed state is the one the grisaille was composed for, not a temporary condition of storage.
questions.hint: Ask what the object is made of, and what the grey painting is pretending that it is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A predella read as a sequence
questions.learningObjective: explain how a predella sequences episodes around a main panel
questions.stem: Beneath a large enthroned figure a strip of five small scenes runs left to right in a single continuous moulding, each with its own plain landscape and the same building repeated behind. What is the strip doing?

options.text: Sequencing episodes of one story, so that the main panel above is read as the point the episodes lead to
Presenting a second sacred scene, so that the strip carries weight equal to the panel above it
options.misconception: mistakes a narrative sequence for a competing main subject

options.text: Showing the patron's properties, since the repeated building identifies the estates that paid for it
options.misconception: reads a repeated backdrop as a record of landholdings

options.text: Filling the space beneath the frame, since a wide moulding needed a plain apron below it
options.misconception: treats a narrative strip as a purely structural or decorative filler

questions.explanation: The repeated building and the consistent light tie the five scenes into one continuous world rather than five unrelated illustrations, and the long horizontal format with a moulding that does not change at the internal divisions encourages the eye to read them as a strip, in order, like a sequence of scenes on a frieze. This is the point of the arrangement. The main panel above is a single moment, often a static and iconic one, and a static image has no plot; the predella supplies the plot and therefore supplies the terms in which the main panel is understood. It is not a second main subject competing for attention, since its small scale marks it as subordinate, and the repeated backdrop is a continuity device rather than a list of properties or a strip of plain ornament.
questions.hint: Ask why the same building appears behind all five scenes, and what the eye does with a long strip.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A band of secco loss on a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: read the location of loss as evidence of the painting method
questions.stem: A wall painting is complete across its figures and main areas, but a border of foliage and a line of fine lettering are gone, the losses running as a band along the top of the wall. What does the pattern of loss indicate?

options.text: That the missing work was laid onto dry plaster, so it was never bonded into the wall itself
That a later owner cut the border away, since the losses have sharp and perfectly regular edges
options.misconception: treats regular loss as deliberate removal, ignoring the method it follows from

options.text: That the upper wall was repainted and the earlier work beneath it was scraped off
options.misconception: assumes a campaign of repainting where the evidence shows a technique difference

options.text: That a scaffold stood across the top, so the loss is the shadow the scaffold left behind
options.misconception: invents a physical cause, where the loss follows the method of application

questions.explanation: Where a wall has lost paint, the shape of the loss is usually a fact about the method rather than about damage. Foliage, gilding-like detail and the small lettering of an inscription were among the first things a fresco painter added after the plaster had dried, because lime will not take a fine line, a bright opaque colour or a metallic leaf. Those secco passages sit on the surface as a film, nothing under them joins them to the wall, and they are consequently the first layers to go when the wall is touched, damped or salt-affected. The main figures, painted into wet plaster, survive because they are the wall. The band's regularity reflects the uniform treatment of a top border, not a cut edge, and no repainting or scaffolding is required to explain it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the lost details could not be painted into wet plaster, and what that does to their grip.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mirror that includes the viewer
questions.learningObjective: interpret a convex mirror reflection as a claim about the viewer
questions.stem: A picture shows a dark room lit by one window on the left, a table with a fruit dish, and a small convex mirror on the back wall in which the window appears as a bright disc with two figures standing in the space in front of the picture. What is at work?

options.text: The reflection places the viewer inside the room, so the picture includes whoever stands before it
The detail in the reflection certifies the room, since it was painted from direct observation at that hour
options.misconception: reads the reflection as documentary, forgetting the room is invented too

options.text: The mirror enlarges the interior, doubling the space behind the back wall into a further room
options.misconception: believes painted glass adds real space rather than being part of the image

options.text: The bright reflection gives the room a second light, so the interior is genuinely lit from two sides
options.misconception: treats the reflection as a light source, which is what an actual mirror is not

questions.explanation: A convex mirror is the only mirror that sees a whole room from a small disc on the back wall, and it is therefore the device for making a picture refer to the space in front of itself. Once the reflected window and the two figures are inside that disc, the room in the painting is closed and the viewer is placed in it, looking at a picture that has already included them. The interior remains entirely invented, so the reflection certifies nothing about a real room, and the hours the picture was painted in say nothing about the hours it depicts. Nor is anything enlarged: the glass is painted, and it reports light rather than producing it, so the room still has the one window that lit it.
questions.hint: Ask what only a convex mirror can gather into its small disc, and who is standing in the answer.
