questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An attribute changed under the paint
questions.learningObjective: read an altered attribute as evidence of a changed decision
questions.stem: Examination of a religious panel finds, beneath the paint, a pair of wings on the figure's shoulders and a different shape for the object at its feet. The finished picture shows neither. What does this establish?

options.text: That the attribute was altered in the paint, so what the picture now says about the figure is not its first decision
That two workshops painted the panel, since the earlier figure belonged to a picture now lost
options.misconception: jumps to a second campaign without showing that the layers are one campaign

options.text: That the image is a copy, since the outline was traced from an engraving made somewhere else
options.misconception: assumes a printed source, where the altered drawing is under this panel's own paint

options.text: That a restorer removed them, substituting a plainer type for the figure that was there
options.misconception: blames a later intervention, ignoring that the paint itself covers the first design

questions.explanation: An attribute is the viewer's means of knowing which figure is meant, so changing one is a serious change of subject rather than a revision of a sleeve. The evidence here is the ordinary evidence of alteration: the first design survives under the paint because the layers that buried it differ in thickness and in binding, so examination separates them. What that establishes is a change of mind, made by a hand working on the picture while it was still open to change, and it makes the finished image a decision rather than a starting point. It does not follow that a second painter was involved, that the design came from a print, or that anyone later removed anything, since in each of those cases the difference would lie outside the paint layers of this panel.
questions.hint: Ask what an attribute does for a viewer, and what must have happened for it to change.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A report listing the layers of a panel
questions.learningObjective: interpret a layer sequence as a record of working order
questions.stem: An examination report on a fifteenth-century panel lists, in the order found: a chalk ground, a transferred drawing, a warm stained layer, a light tempera model, transparent glazes over the shadows, and a yellowed resinous coating on top. What does the sequence establish?

options.text: The order of the working process, from preparation through modelling and glazing to a coating applied later
That two painters worked on the panel, since a tempera model and oil glazes require different hands
options.misconception: reads a change of medium as a change of painter, which the layers do not show

options.text: That the picture was copied from a print, since the transferred design came from elsewhere
options.misconception: assumes a printed source, where the transfer simply moves a drawing onto the ground

options.text: That the light model is a separate study, and the picture is a later enlarged version of it
options.misconception: mistakes a layer within the picture for a preliminary object in its own right

questions.explanation: Each entry is a layer on the panel, and layers are laid in order, so the list is a stratigraphy and therefore a record of how the picture was made. The chalk ground had to exist before anything could be drawn on it. The transferred design had to be on that ground before any colour was committed. The warm stain sets a tone and comes before the modelling that will sit on it. The light tempera model is the forms, and the glazes are transparent films that could only be laid over a model already dry enough to take them. The resinous coating sits on top of all of it and, being yellowed and separable from the rest, is a later addition rather than part of the original sequence. None of this distinguishes hands, and a transferred design is not a printed one.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be dry and in place before the next layer can be laid on it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A single-campaign claim tested against the panel
questions.learningObjective: weigh a catalogue claim against the material evidence
questions.stem: A catalogue describes a panel as the work of one hand painted in a single campaign. Examination finds a transferred cartoon whose drapery folds are struck through and repainted, and a warm stained layer absent from the shadow passages. What does this do to the claim?

options.text: It leaves one campaign plausible but complicates the account, since design and tone were both revised in the paint
It refutes the single hand, because any revision on a panel must belong to a second painter
options.misconception: assumes a revision implies a second artist, which is not what it shows

options.text: It proves the panel is an assembly, since a transferred cartoon cannot survive on a made support
options.misconception: draws a structural conclusion from a transfer, which transfers perfectly well

options.text: It dates the work later, because revisions on a panel can only be recent additions to it
options.misconception: assumes a revision is modern, ignoring revisions made while the picture was open

questions.explanation: A single campaign means the picture was brought to its finished state in one continuous process, and the evidence here is consistent with that: the transferred cartoon, the warm stain and the repainted folds all belong to the making rather than to a later addition, because they lie inside the paint film and show the design being changed while the panel was still open. What the evidence does undermine is any claim that the picture came out of the ground fully resolved. The catalogue's account has to be rewritten, not its attribution reversed. A revision is the normal condition of a painting in progress, it says nothing about the number of hands, and it does not imply that the panel is a composite object or that the picture is modern.
questions.hint: Ask whether the changes lie inside the paint film or on top of it, and what that says about when they were made.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A support that has been transferred
questions.learningObjective: identify a transferred support from the object's own evidence
questions.stem: A record describes a picture as oil on canvas. The object in front of the examiner is a wooden panel, but a strip of linen is tacked across a horizontal joint on its reverse, and the paint on the front is a thin film carried by that cloth. What does the object say?

options.text: That a canvas was transferred to a panel, so the record's support and medium describe an earlier state of the work
That the linen is a repair, and the picture was painted straight onto the wood beneath it
options.misconception: takes the cloth for a patch, where a paint film on the cloth says otherwise

options.text: That the panel is a later backing, and the picture was always painted on the cloth alone
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the transfer, which the paint film settles

options.text: That the linen was cut from here for analysis, and its position proves nothing about the front
options.misconception: assumes the strip is a sample, when it lies under the paint on the picture's face

questions.explanation: The direction of a transfer is fixed by where the paint sits relative to the cloth. Paint applied last is the outermost layer of the object, so if the linen lies beneath the paint film on the front of the panel, the cloth is older than the paint and the painting was made on the cloth and afterwards moved to the wood. That is a common history for a picture, since a badly moving canvas may be removed from its stretcher and laid down on a panel, sometimes with the old joins reinforced, and it changes nothing about how the picture looks. So the record's description of an early state, and the support named in it belongs to the picture's past rather than its present. A patch would not carry a paint film, and a strip lying on the reverse of a panel has told the examiner which surface the picture was made on.
questions.hint: Ask which surface the paint film is on, and whether the cloth lies above it or below it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A stratigraphic report on a wall
questions.learningObjective: read a wall's layer sequence as evidence of mixed method
questions.stem: A report on a wall painting records, in order: a rough plaster coat, a red-brown drawing, a fine pale plaster coat, the main figures, and then thin films of colour and gold leaf that sit above the plaster surface in a band along the top. What does this establish?

options.text: That the wall was built and painted in true fresco, and the top band was added afterwards onto dry plaster
That the whole wall was painted a secco, since one secco passage at the top proves a single method
options.misconception: generalises from the band to the whole wall, which the buried figures contradict

options.text: That the main figures were painted a secco, since they lie over a fine coat rather than a rough one
options.misconception: misreads the plaster sequence, since the fine coat is what the fresco figures sit in

options.text: That the gold was fused into the plaster wet, since the films lie against the plaster surface
options.misconception: reads a layer sitting above the plaster as one fused into it

questions.explanation: The sequence is the standard one for a fresco wall. The rough coat receives the red drawing, the fine coat is then laid over that drawing and the figures are painted into it while it is damp, which is what binds the colour into the wall. The decisive detail is the last entry. Films that sit above the plaster surface are not in it, so they were applied to a dry wall: gold leaf and fine opaque colour are things lime will not take, and they were added afterwards by a route that has nothing to hold them but a binder. So the wall is mixed in method, which is ordinary practice and not a defect. The presence of a secco band says nothing about the buried figures, and lying on the surface is the opposite of being fused into the plaster.
questions.hint: Ask what tells you whether a colour is inside the wall or sitting on it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An all-fresco claim tested at the border
questions.learningObjective: refute a method claim using the material evidence
questions.stem: A catalogue states that a wall painting was executed entirely in true fresco. Under magnification the fine lettering in the border turns out to be coloured particles held in a glossy film sitting above the plaster surface, with no lime anywhere in it. What does the material evidence establish?

options.text: That the border was painted a secco, so the catalogue's claim cannot be true of the whole wall
That the whole wall was painted a secco, since one secco passage proves the method used throughout
options.misconception: generalises from a border to the whole wall, which the buried figures exclude

options.text: That the wall was cleaned recently, since a glossy film on the surface comes only from varnish
options.misconception: reads any surface film as varnish, ignoring that this film carries the pigment

options.text: That the lettering is modern, since wet plaster would have taken the colour if it were original
options.misconception: concludes a modern date from a method, which the material cannot supply

questions.explanation: The claim is universal and the evidence is local, which is enough to defeat it. In true fresco the pigment is held inside the plaster, so it is part of the wall and shows no separate film; here the colour sits in a glossy layer on the surface with no lime in it at all, which is a binder-bound film and therefore a secco passage. The catalogue sentence is now false as written, and it has to be rewritten to cover the wall in two methods. It does not follow that the buried figures are secco as well, that a varnish has been applied, or that the lettering is recent, since none of those is what the film is. A technical description of a wall should always be checked at its thinnest passages, because that is where the method shows itself.
questions.hint: Ask where a fresco pigment physically is, and where the pigment in the border physically is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A condition survey of an unstable panel
questions.learningObjective: interpret condition data as a measurement problem
questions.stem: A survey of one panel records thirty-four small losses, a widest crack of two millimetres, nineteen years spent on an uninsulated trolley in an unheated corridor before 1975, and a note that crack widths are still increasing. What does the survey establish?

options.text: That the panel is still moving, and the recorded figures give a baseline for measuring whether that stops
That the corridor years caused all the loss, since the losses cluster where the trolley stood
options.misconception: attributes every defect to one period, which the record does not distribute

options.text: That a warmer room would settle the panel, since wood moves less as the temperature rises
options.misconception: assumes a direction of movement, when the panel responds to changes in both

options.text: That the painting is beyond saving, since a crack that is widening cannot be arrested at all
options.misconception: jumps from continued movement to hopelessness, which the evidence does not support

questions.explanation: The decisive entry is the last one. Movement that has not stopped is the whole problem, because a panel that is still opening its cracks will keep doing so whatever is done to its surface, and treatment has to begin with controlling the cause rather than with the paint. Counting the losses and measuring the cracks is what converts that statement into something actionable: thirty-four losses and a two-millimetre crack are figures that can be counted again in five years, and any change in them will show whether the environment has been stabilised. A single historical period cannot account for damage of several kinds, and warming a room is not the same as stabilising it, since what a panel responds to is change rather than level. Continued movement is a reason for intervention, not a verdict on the picture.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four entries is a measurement you could take again, and which is a trend.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Consolidating a secco passage
questions.learningObjective: carry a technical difference through to a treatment decision
questions.stem: A conservator must decide whether to consolidate a secco passage on a fresco wall. First say why that passage is held less firmly than the figures beside it, and then say what the difference implies for the treatment.

options.text: It is a film sitting on the surface with nothing bonding it into the wall, so consolidating means re-adhering something that may lift again
It is attached more strongly than the fresco, so the passage can safely be cleaned before anything is done to it
options.misconception: inverts the adhesion, treating a surface film as the more secure layer

options.text: It is the same colour as the plaster, so the decision has to be made on appearance alone
options.misconception: makes a technical problem a matter of colour, ignoring the attachment entirely

options.text: It cannot be examined at all, since a film on plaster is invisible under any available light
options.misconception: assumes the passage is unobservable, when surface films read easily

questions.explanation: The first answer has to name the mechanism. Fresco pigment is trapped in the plaster's own structure as the lime sets, so the picture and the wall are one body; a secco passage is a layer of pigment in a binder that dried on the surface, and its grip is whatever the binder managed to hold. From that the treatment follows, and it is a two-part problem. Re-adhesing is possible and is often done, but it is not a repair of the wall's structure, so it can fail again with the next cycle of damp, salt movement or handling. The durable work is environmental and structural: stabilise the plaster, control the salts, control who touches the wall. Anyone who consolidates without doing that has bought time rather than permanence.
questions.hint: Ask where the pigment of each method physically sits, and what the difference is worth to a treatment plan.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Using a pentimento without over-reading it
questions.learningObjective: separate what a pentimento evidences from what it does not
questions.stem: A portrait carries a pentimento showing a hat that is not the sitter's. First say what that evidences about the making of the picture, and then say what it cannot tell you about the reason for the change.

options.text: It evidences a design revised on the panel, but not whether the change was for the sitter, the patron or the studio's convenience
It evidences two hands working on the panel, but not which of them set down the first design
options.misconception: turns a revision into a second artist, which is not what the trace shows

options.text: It evidences a design taken from a print, but not whether that print can still be identified
options.misconception: assumes a printed source, which a pentimento does not imply

options.text: It evidences that the picture is a copy of an earlier version, but not where that version was kept
options.misconception: reads a revision as dependence on another picture, which is a different claim

questions.explanation: A pentimento is a fact about sequence and nothing else. It establishes that a design stood on this panel and was then replaced, that the replacement was made while the paint was still workable, and that the hand that made it was working on the picture rather than copying one that already existed. Those are the uses a conservator makes of it: reading the earlier composition, dating the change to the working period, and correcting older descriptions of what the picture shows. The motives are a different order of question. A hat might have been removed because the sitter disliked it, because a member of the family did, because it was impractical in the workshop, or for reasons nobody recorded, and the paint cannot arbitrate between them. The temptation is always to supply a story; the discipline is to stop where the material stops.
questions.hint: Ask what the layer difference can date, and whether it can date a motive.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The risk in removing a varnish
questions.learningObjective: connect a glaze's dependence on its underlayer to a cleaning risk
questions.stem: A conservator proposes to remove a discoloured varnish from a panel whose shadows are built from transparent oil glazes. First say what a glaze depends on, and then say what removing the coating puts at risk.

options.text: A glaze depends on the pale layer beneath it for its colour, so stripping the coating can carry the modelling away with it
A glaze is independent of what is under it, so the modelling is untouched by anything laid over it
options.misconception: assumes a glaze is self-sufficient, which is what a glaze is not

options.text: A glaze is the topmost layer of the picture, so there is nothing at all between it and the varnish
options.misconception: puts the glaze at the surface, forgetting the layers it is built over

options.text: A glaze only affects the shine, so the risk to the picture is dullness rather than any loss of paint
options.misconception: reduces the risk to appearance, ignoring that the film carries colour

questions.explanation: A transparent film has no colour of its own worth speaking of; it works because it is thin, and because what is under it is there to be seen through it and lit back through. The pale model built in tempera is not a preliminary sketch but the reflector that makes the whole passage work, and it is usually far more fragile than the surface film. So a cleaning that is perfectly safe on an opaque panel, where the top layer is a solid body of paint, becomes a risk on a glazed one, where solvent that dissolves a resin can also lift a soft, thin, poorly bound film. That is why the treatment decision is made on a small cleaned area and examined, and why the proposal must be argued against the alternative of leaving the varnish, which is reversible and the coating is not.
questions.hint: Ask where the colour of a glazed passage actually is, and which of the two layers is the sturdier one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an eye-level horizon obliges a hanging to do
questions.learningObjective: carry a pictorial convention through to the hanging of a picture
questions.stem: A picture's horizon is set at the height of the viewer's eye. First say what that does to the painted space, and then say what it obliges the hanging of the picture to preserve.

options.text: It matches the real eye so the painted floor continues the room's floor, so the picture has to be hung at the height it was made for
It raises the painted floor above the real one, so the picture may be hung anywhere in the room
options.misconception: reverses the effect, and with it frees the hanging when it is not free

options.text: It flattens the painted space, so the frame can be set flush against the wall it hangs on
options.misconception: treats a matched eye level as a flattening, which is the opposite

options.text: It removes the need for a horizon, so the picture can be rehung at any height at all
options.misconception: claims the horizon is unnecessary, where it is the thing being matched

questions.explanation: The convention only works if the two eye levels are the same, so the second half of the answer is about what a hanging has to do. A viewer in a gallery stands and looks forward, and the height at which they look is set by the picture's centre in their field of vision and by their own stature. Hang a low-horizoned picture high and the painted floor now lies below the real floor of the room, the viewer looks down on the scene, and the illusion of a space continuing through the wall collapses; hang it low and the effect is a floor rising towards you. This is a real constraint in rooms where works are hung on a uniform line, and it is one reason pictures built around a specific eye level have traditionally wanted a specific position. The horizon is not removed by being matched; matching is what gives it meaning.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye level of the room is, and what happens to the painted floor if the two no longer agree.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of work on a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a true fresco wall
questions.stem: A wall is to be painted in true fresco. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Add the fine detail in gold leaf and in secco colour, once the wall has dried
Lay the rough plaster coat that is to receive the design
Draw the design onto that coat in red earth, and leave it to dry
Lay the fresh fine plaster and paint the figures into it while it is still damp

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each stage needs from the one before. The rough coat exists to be drawn on, and it has to be there before the drawing is made, since the drawing on the red layer is the design the painter will follow and the one a restorer will find if the colour is lost. The fine coat then goes over that drawing, and it has to be laid and painted in one operation, because its being damp is the only thing that will bind the pigment to the wall. Gold leaf and fine colour come last because lime will not take them and because they are added to a surface that must already be there. The daily joins in the wall fall between the third stage and the end, since the fine coat is laid one patch at a time as it is painted.
questions.hint: Ask which stage needs the one before it to be dry, and which needs it to be wet.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of work on a tempera and oil panel
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a tempera and oil panel painting
questions.stem: A panel painting is to be made in egg tempera and finished in oil. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Apply a thin resinous coating over the dry picture and leave the panel ready to be seen
Sand the gesso, transfer the design onto it, and stain the ground with a warm imprimatura
Size the wood with glue and build up the gesso in thin layers, drying and sanding between them
Model the forms in a light egg tempera and then deepen the shadows with transparent oil glazes

questions.explanation: Every stage is a condition for the next. The bare panel cannot take anything until glue has sealed it, and it cannot take a drawn line or a flat surface until the gesso has been built up and sanded, so the ground is first. On the ground the design is transferred, because a design fixed before colour can still be corrected and a design traced onto wet paint cannot; the warm imprimatura follows on the same prepared surface, thin enough to be seen through. The painting then comes in two passes, a light tempera model and oil glazes over it, in that order because the glazes need a dry, light, opaque underlayer to work against. The coating goes last, when the paint beneath is hard enough to be covered and needs protecting from handling and from the air.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be sealed, what has to be flat, and what has to be dry before the glazes go on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order from outdoor study to finished picture
questions.learningObjective: sequence the use of an outdoor study in a finished picture
questions.stem: A painter is turning a small outdoor study into a finished picture. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Work up the glazes and the final highlights, and compare the finished light against the site again
Note the light, the sky and the arrangement of the forms on the spot, before any of them change
Carry that record back and lay in the main masses of the finished composition in the studio
Make the rapid painted or drawn record on the spot, while the conditions just noted still hold

questions.explanation: The order follows from what decays fastest. Light and weather change within the hour, so they have to be observed and written down at the site before anything else is attempted, while the arrangement of the forms, which lasts for days, is recorded afterwards and more slowly. Only then can the record be used, and the use is a reorganisation: the study is a small thing with a single viewpoint and no room to correct, so the finished picture takes from it the specific values, the sky, and the exact light, while the composition itself is laid in at a larger scale where changes are still cheap. Glazes and highlights are last, because they depend on an underlying structure that has to be settled first, and the final comparison against the site is what catches a studio light that has quietly drifted away from the one recorded.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the observed scene change within the hour, and what the study is later used for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a technical investigation
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that establish a painting's layers
questions.stem: Before a panel painting is treated, its layers have to be established. Put these four steps into the order in which a conservator must take them.

options.text: Sample the paint and the ground so that the materials can be identified in the laboratory
Examine the surface in raking, ultraviolet and infrared light, and record every loss, fill and crack
Map the sequence of layers across the picture, from the transferred drawing to the surface coating
Write a condition report and set out the options for treatment, with the risk of each one stated

questions.explanation: Treatment is irreversible and sampling is not, so the sequence runs from the least invasive to the most. Examination comes first because it is entirely non-destructive and it tells the conservator where the losses, fills and previous campaigns are, which determines where anything should be taken. The layer map follows, since it needs the surface record and the sequences it revealed to know where a sample would be informative rather than merely destructive. Then the samples, in the smallest number that will answer the question, because each one is a hole. The report and the options come last, and they are written with the risk of each option stated, including the option of doing nothing, which is frequently the correct one. Nothing is proposed before the object has been read.
questions.hint: Ask which steps change the object and which only look at it, and put the irreversible ones last.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a secco passage outlives nothing
questions.learningObjective: explain the adhesion difference between buon fresco and secco
questions.stem: Explain why a passage painted onto dry plaster is less durable than one painted into wet plaster, stating the physical reason and the consequences for the wall.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the chemistry, because the whole difference is chemical. Fresh lime plaster is a mass of calcium hydroxide that is still wet and still reactive. When pigment is brushed into it, and as the wall dries, the lime reacts with carbon dioxide from the air and converts to a hard carbonate. The conversion happens throughout the thickness of the plaster, including around the pigment grains, so the colour ends up enclosed inside the new crystalline structure. The picture and the wall become one body: a passage painted this way can only be lost by losing the wall itself. A secco passage is different in kind. The plaster has already set and is chemically inert, and the pigment is held in a binder such as animal glue, wax or oil that dries as a film lying on the surface. That film has no mechanical or chemical attachment to the wall; it is held by surface adhesion, by whatever slight key of the plaster's texture, and by nothing more. Set out the consequences and they follow. The secco film is the most exposed layer on the wall, so it takes handling, abrasion, condensation and the movement of the wall in front of it, and it is the first thing to go. It is also the first to go from salts drawn through the plaster, since a film that is not bonded allows the salt solution to get underneath and lift it. The loss looks dramatic, because a missing frieze of foliage or a line of lettering interrupts an otherwise complete picture, and restorers are reluctant to replace it: the original binder is gone, any substitute is a modern addition, and a retouched passage is a permanent mark on an old wall. Note finally that this is not a criticism of the technique. Lime will not take a fine line, a bright opaque colour, a glaze, or gold leaf, and painters added all of these a secco throughout the period, knowing what they were doing. A wall may be entirely mixed in method without being faulty, and the best description of any particular passage is the one that states which kind it is.

questions.explanation: A full answer names the carbonation of lime as the mechanism that encloses the pigment, states that a secco film is merely sitting on an inert surface, and derives the greater vulnerability from that attachment difference. A weak response says only that secco is less good, or attributes it to a poor binder without saying what the wall is doing.
questions.hint: Ask what the lime is doing chemically as it dries, and where a glued pigment actually sits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pentimento can and cannot be used for
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the evidentiary value of a pentimento
questions.stem: Explain what a pentimento proves about how a painting was made, and set out where a reader must stop rather than go on inventing.

answer.exemplar: Start by saying what a pentimento is physically. A painter blocks in one form, then decides differently, then paints over the first. What survives is a difference between two adjacent paint layers: the buried one is usually thicker, differently bound or differently coloured, so that light, infrared or X-ray examination separates the two and the earlier outline reads through the later one. Name what that licenses. It establishes a sequence: this design stood on this panel, at this stage, and was replaced while the paint was still open to work. From it a conservator can reconstruct the earlier composition, correct older published descriptions of what the picture shows, and show that the picture was arrived at rather than copied, since a hand revising its own work is a different act from a hand following one. It also gives a terminus: the revision is inside the working period, not a later addition. Then say where it stops, which is the half of the question most answers miss. The material difference dates a decision and nothing about the reason for it. A hat may have been removed because the sitter changed their mind, because a member of the family forbade it, because the workshop found the wide brim awkward to model, or for reasons no record survives. The paint does not choose between these, and any narrative built on it is a narrative the reader has supplied. Two further errors are common. One is to convert a revision into a second artist, as though a changed design always meant a second hand, when a single hand changes designs as often as it keeps them. The other is to treat the trace as proof of dependence on another picture or on a print, which requires a transferred outline to be shown, not merely an altered one. Set out the discipline, then: read the pentimento for the sequence and the design, report the motive as unknown, and say so in the catalogue so that the next reader does not have to guess either.

questions.explanation: A full answer defines the pentimento as a difference between two paint layers, draws the inferences about sequence and date, and then explicitly marks the boundary at motive, hand and source. A weak response either treats any ghost image as proof of a second campaign or invents a story for the change.
questions.hint: Ask what a layer difference can date, and then ask what it cannot date.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a glaze looks deep and what its loss costs
questions.learningObjective: explain the optics of glazing and the consequence of its removal
questions.stem: Explain how a transparent glaze produces a sense of depth in a colour, and what is lost from a picture when a glaze is taken away in cleaning.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the light path, since the whole effect is optical and not material. A glaze is a layer of colour so thin that it stays transparent: no pigment is opaque, and there is no opaque body of colour sitting on the surface. Light enters the film, passes through it, reaches the pale paint beneath, is scattered and reflected back, and passes out through the film again, picking up the film's colour on the way. What reaches the eye is therefore light that has been tinted twice, once on the way in and once on the way out, and the viewer reads that as a colour being generated beneath the surface rather than reflected from it. That is what depth means in a picture. It is also why glazing is additive: several thin films of the same hue deepen the passage almost indefinitely while remaining transparent, so a shadow can be built to a degree of richness no single opaque mixture reaches, and it is why a glazed passage reads differently from a mixed one even when the two look the same on the palette. Now take the other half. The colour of a glazed passage is not in the glaze. It is in the light layer beneath, which is usually a pale tempera model, thin, softly bound and less durable than the surface film that covers it. So a cleaning strong enough to lift the coating can lift the modelling with it, and the loss is not merely a duller surface: the shadow comes away and leaves a flat, light, dead passage, because the thing that was reflecting light upward is gone. Two practical consequences follow. A conservator cannot treat a glazed panel as though its top layer were solid paint, which is why cleaning is tested on a small area and examined before it proceeds, and why a heavily glazed picture is often left with its varnish in place despite the discolouration, since a discoloured coating is a reversible problem and the removal of the modelling is not. Note too that the two failures are different in kind: an over-cleaned passage has lost information permanently, whereas a yellowed varnish can be dealt with later if the risk is judged worth taking.

questions.explanation: A full answer describes the double passage of light through a transparent film, connects that to the perception of depth, and then shows that the colour of the passage resides in the fragile underlayer, which is what a cleaning risks. A weak response says only that glazes look rich, without the light path or the loss.
questions.hint: Ask how many times light is tinted on its way in and out of a transparent film.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish changes the reading of a picture
questions.learningObjective: explain how a later coating alters the appearance that is evidence
questions.stem: Explain how a varnish applied long after a picture was painted changes what a viewer sees, and what a restorer has to establish before removing one.

answer.exemplar: Start with what the coating physically is. A varnish is a resin dissolved in oil or solvent, brushed over the dry paint and left to cure into a film, and it does two jobs: it gives the surface a gloss that deepens the darks and increases the apparent saturation of the colours, and it protects the paint from handling, dust and the air. Both jobs are altered by age. The resin oxidises and yellows, and a yellow film over a picture is a filter: light going into the paint is tinted on the way in and again on the way out, so warm lights shift towards brown and greens, blues and violets lose their freshness. Because the film is transparent and thickest where the picture is darkest, the effect is uneven, and the shadows take the heaviest dulling while the highlights, seen through the thinnest film, look comparatively clean. A viewer is therefore not looking at the colours the painter mixed. That is the first half of the answer, and it is the reason the question matters beyond tidiness: the evidence a painting offers about its maker is filtered through a material addition. Now the second half. Before a coating is removed, a restorer has to establish what the picture looks like without it, which means establishing how the paint is built and how firmly. If the shadows are made of transparent glazes over a thin pale underpainting, the modelling lives in fragile layers beneath and a solvent that dissolves the resin can take them too. So the examination is non-destructive and comes first: raking light for the impasto, ultraviolet for the coating and for old retouching, infrared for the drawing beneath, and a small cleaned test area examined before any further work. The point to end on is the asymmetry. Removing a varnish is irreversible and takes with it whatever it was holding, while leaving a yellowed one in place is a decision that can be reviewed in twenty years when the technique will be better. Restraint is not ignorance of the damage; it is a judgement about which damage can be undone.

questions.explanation: A full answer explains the coating as a coloured filter that alters the colours the viewer sees, unevenly across the picture, and then lists the non-destructive examinations that must precede a removal decision. A weak response says only that varnish makes colours warmer, with nothing about the risk to the paint.
questions.hint: Ask what a transparent yellow film does to light on its way in and on its way out, and what has to be known before it is taken off.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Counting the giornate on a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: compute the number of working sections from a daily area
questions.stem: A chapel wall of 48 square metres is painted in true fresco. A surviving record states that each day's section of fresh plaster covered 6 square metres, and the wall is painted without a break. How many working days did the wall take?
questions.explanation: The number of days is the area divided by the area covered in a day: 48 divided by 6 is 8, and 8 multiplied by 6 returns the 48, so the two routes agree. The division is a plain one but the unit matters, since the giornate are patches of wet plaster whose size is set by how much a painter can lay and paint before the plaster stops being workable, and that area rather than the wall's height or width is what determines the count. It follows that the daily joins in the finished wall mark the boundaries of those 8 sections, and that a restorer counting surviving joins can check the record. A wall painted half in fresco and half with a coat of plaster applied and painted in a single day would have fewer joins than this count implies.
questions.hint: Put the two areas in the same units and divide the total by the amount covered each day.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading depth from the drawn size of equal squares
questions.learningObjective: compute a depth ratio from a perspective construction
questions.stem: In a perspective construction the square of pavement nearest the viewer is drawn 20 cm across and the square three rows further back is drawn 5 cm across. In linear perspective the drawn size of an equal square falls in proportion to its distance from the picture plane. How many times further from the picture plane does the far square lie than the near one?
questions.explanation: In a perspective construction two squares of the same real size are drawn in inverse proportion to their distance from the picture plane, so the ratio of the drawn sizes is the reciprocal of the ratio of the distances. Dividing the larger drawn size by the smaller gives 20 divided by 5, which is 4, and the inverse of that is one quarter, so the far square must lie four times as far away as the near one. The same figure can be checked the other way: if each row takes a constant factor of reduction, that factor is the cube root of 4, about 1.587, and applying it for the three rows from 5 cm returns 20 cm. Two consequences are worth stating. A drawn size of 2.5 cm would place the square eight times further off, and a halving of the drawn size doubles the distance, which is the practical rule painters use when testing a construction.
questions.hint: The drawn size and the distance vary inversely, so divide the drawn sizes and take the reciprocal.
